subject: Accounting
title: Gathering Evidence
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Gathering Evidence.

hook.text: An auditor doesn't just trust the company's numbers. They demand proof.

buildup.text: Audit evidence comes from documents, bank confirmations, physical inspections, and recalculations.

discovery.text: External evidence—like a bank statement—is more reliable than internal documents the company created.

twist.text: Parmalat forged a bank confirmation letter. Even evidence has to be verified for authenticity.

climax.text: The quality and quantity of evidence determines whether the auditor can form a solid opinion.

punchline.text: No evidence, no opinion. Auditors deal in proof.

quiz.question: Which type of audit evidence is most reliable?

details.summary: Audit evidence is the information auditors collect to support their opinion on financial statements — including documents, confirmations, observations, and analytical procedures. More persuasive evidence is required for higher-risk areas.
details.whyItMatters: The quality and sufficiency of audit evidence directly determines whether an auditor's opinion is well-founded. Insufficient evidence leads to unreliable conclusions and potential audit failure.
takeaways: Audit evidence includes inspection of documents, external confirmations, recalculations, and observations
Evidence from independent external sources is more reliable than internally generated documents
Higher-risk areas require more evidence and more persuasive types of evidence

faq.question: What types of audit evidence do auditors collect?
faq.answer: Auditors use inspection (examining documents), observation (watching processes), inquiry (asking questions), confirmation (verifying with third parties), recalculation (re-performing math), and analytical procedures (comparing trends). Combining types provides stronger assurance.

faq.question: Why is external evidence considered more reliable than internal evidence?
faq.answer: External evidence — like bank confirmations or supplier invoices — comes from parties independent of the company being audited, who have no incentive to misrepresent. Internal documents could potentially be altered or fabricated by management. Independent evidence provides stronger assurance.
